case20v1-bm.marketplace:
Jivhala: Spending the Weeks Before Diwali

A decision case on marketplace economics, Pune, October 2026

1. Opening

At 5:00 p.m. on Monday 19 October 2026, Sandhya Chaubal closed the September numbers in Jivhala's office in Baner, Pune, and opened a message from the chief executive. Sulochana Chendvankar wanted one recommendation by Friday 23 October: how Jivhala should spend the weeks before Diwali, which falls on Sunday 8 November, when repair and deep-cleaning requests climb every year. Whatever was chosen had to be live on Monday 26 October, and the message asked that the memo name a single option, its cost in rupees and the month in which it would show results.

The headline was good. Jivhala had processed ₹109.90 lakh of gross merchandise value (GMV) in September, meaning what households paid for completed jobs. But Chaubal, the vice-president of product, had stopped trusting GMV as the number that mattered. One line in the pack bothered her: active providers had fallen from 1,105 in August to 1,000.

2. Company background

Chendvankar, a former product manager, founded Jivhala in 2021 to connect Pune households with electricians, plumbers, AC technicians and carpenters. A household posts a request; the nearest suitable provider accepts; the household pays by UPI through Razorpay; and Jivhala keeps a commission and settles the rest to the provider's bank account every week. By September 2026 it employed about 140 people, mostly in Pune, and had raised ₹60 crore across two rounds. It operates in five micro-markets: Kothrud, Baner-Aundh, Hinjewadi-Wakad, Hadapsar-Magarpatta and Kharadi-Viman Nagar.

Providers are mostly self-employed technicians who also take private work, so the app is one source of income among several. Competition is layered. Urban Company, the national leader, positions itself as a curated, premium service. Pune's housing societies run WhatsApp groups that recommend a trusted plumber for nothing. And every provider keeps the phone numbers of households they have served. Jivhala charges households only the job price and charges providers a commission of 20 per cent of it.

3. The situation

Chaubal convened a call at 5:00 p.m. Samruddhi Chogale, the data scientist, joined from Toronto at 7:30 a.m.; Sarang Chopade, the customer-success lead, from Singapore at 7:30 p.m.

Exhibit 1 sets out September by zone. Households posted 19,000 requests and 10,990 became completed jobs. The share varied from 75.0 per cent in Kothrud to 40.0 per cent in Kharadi-Viman Nagar, and so did the jobs each active provider completed, from 15.0 to 7.0. Marketing spend by zone, ₹12.00 lakh in all, sits beside them. Exhibit 2 follows providers between August and September; the 85 who joined or returned did not offset the 190 who stopped. Of 1,105 active in August, 190 completed no job in September, and the loss ranged from 8.1 per cent of a zone's August providers in Baner-Aundh to 28.2 per cent in Kharadi-Viman Nagar.

Exhibit 3 shows what one average job earns. Jivhala keeps ₹200 of a ₹1,000 job and, after payment processing, refunds and support, ₹125. Figure 1 converts jobs into what a provider receives from the app each month. Chopade had reached 41 of the 190 leavers, those who agreed to talk, not a random sample; the figure they quoted most often as the minimum worth staying for was ₹9,000 a month, and the dashed line marks it. He noted that a provider who takes a household's number can charge ₹900 for the same job, keeping all of it, while the household saves ₹100.

Jivhala masks both phone numbers during a job, in keeping with the data-minimisation spirit of the DPDP Act, but numbers still change hands at the doorstep. Chaubal also knew the board watched GMV, that Series B talks were planned for January, and that society managers book deep-cleaning teams weeks ahead of Diwali, so October's requests would be set by what providers could promise now.

4. The people

Sulochana Chendvankar, chief executive, Pune, wants a festive plan that shows growth. Investors read GMV, and she is wary of any option that makes it smaller before January.

Shashank Chaugule, chief operating officer, Pune, runs field operations. He regards the two weakest zones as a drain on management time and marketing money, and wants effort moved to where jobs complete. Last year he closed a depot in Pimpri that never reached density, and he does not see Kharadi differently.

Samruddhi Chogale, data scientist, Toronto, thinks many unfilled requests in the busiest zone ask for skills or time slots that nearby providers do not offer. She has not yet tested this. She wants any change run as a measured trial rather than a city-wide switch.

Sarang Chopade, customer-success lead, Singapore, speaks to leavers every week. He argues that Jivhala is losing the people who do the work, and that nothing else it spends will matter if they go. Several leavers told him they had found too few jobs to cover a month's costs.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: cut the commission. Reduce it from 20 per cent to 12 per cent in every zone for 90 days from 26 October, lifting the provider's payout on a ₹1,000 job from ₹800 to ₹880. At September volume this gives up ₹8.79 lakh of commission a month, about ₹26.4 lakh over the period. It would be announced to providers by WhatsApp on 26 October, and it leaves marketing and onboarding unchanged.

Option B: concentrate. Keep the 20 per cent commission for the same 90 days. Move the ₹4.00 lakh a month of marketing now spent in Hadapsar-Magarpatta and Kharadi-Viman Nagar into the other three zones, stop recruiting providers in the two, and invite their least-busy providers to change home zone, while continuing to serve households who already use the app. Those zones produced 2,620 jobs and ₹26.20 lakh of GMV in September. The option leaves their providers on current terms and accepts a smaller GMV there.

Option C: share the price. For the same 90 days, lower the provider commission to 15 per cent and charge each household a ₹50 booking fee, recorded as Jivhala revenue. At unchanged volume Jivhala still earns ₹200 a job; providers receive ₹850 and households pay ₹1,050. It leaves zones, marketing and onboarding unchanged and puts a new charge in front of every household.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, in which zones does the binding constraint sit with households and in which with providers? What further evidence would you want?
  2. Jivhala calls its 20 per cent a take rate. What is it measured over, what does the board's GMV figure leave out, and who is Jivhala's paying customer?
  3. For each option, what must be true of provider and household behaviour for it to work by 24 January 2027, the end of a 90-day trial from 26 October, and which of those assumptions can the exhibits test?
  4. Which option would you recommend by Friday, what would you watch in the first thirty days, and what result would make you reverse it?

8. A note for the learner

Marketplace economics separates three things that one dashboard blends. GMV measures volume. Take rate is the price Jivhala charges on that volume. Liquidity is the likelihood that a request becomes a completed job, and it is local: a plumber in Kothrud adds nothing for a household in Kharadi. A decision framed by this lens asks what each lever changes in the chain from request to job, and what it costs per job.

One defensible path is Option B, run as a 90-day trial with its limits written down in advance. Commission is a blunt lever that spends contribution in every zone at once, while the zones in this case differ sharply. Concentrating spend tests whether density in three zones can be deepened before the Series B conversation, at the price of a smaller GMV in two. The trial needs its limits fixed in advance: a floor for fill rate and for provider exits in the three zones, a review on day 30, and a date by which the two paused zones are either restarted or formally closed. Chogale's skills-and-slots hypothesis can be checked on the unfilled Hinjewadi-Wakad requests while the trial runs.
case40v1-bm.marketplace:
Kharedi: the rate, the ramp and the twenty

Indian School of Business · Strategy & Business · Business Models · case for class discussion

1. Sunday night, Baner

At twenty to ten on the night of Sunday, 25 October 2026, the second floor of Kharedi Commerce Private Limited on Baner Road in Pune held one person and the security lighting. Tarangini Darekar, who had founded the company seven years earlier with a borrowed laptop and a list of brake-pad distributors, sat with two sheets of paper and could not decide which she believed.

The first was the finance pack her chief financial officer had circulated on Thursday: a staged increase in Kharedi's commission from a blended 4.34 per cent of gross merchandise value to 6.00 per cent, category by category, from November to March. The second was a note from Toronto arguing that the attrition assumption underneath the first was wrong by a factor of two and a half. The board would meet at ten, and the Series C term sheet was conditional on a net-revenue number for the year to 31 March 2027 that Kharedi was not on course to reach.

That morning the clocks in Berlin had gone back, and her design lead there had moved from three and a half hours behind Pune to four and a half. It was the only thing in her week that had settled itself.

2. How Kharedi came to be shaped this way

Kharedi began in March 2019 as a searchable catalogue of automotive spare parts, built because its two founders — Darekar, then twenty-nine, and Tatyasaheb Dhanorkar, who had run a brake-parts distributorship in Kolhapur for nineteen years — could not tell an independent garage in Satara that a part sat on a shelf in Pune. Buyers were multi-brand workshops, parts retailers and small fleet operators; sellers were distributors, rebuilders and manufacturers' regional depots.

Two decisions from that period still bind, and Exhibit 2 places them. In August 2022, to make the marketplace usable to a workshop that had never bought online, Kharedi began paying the freight itself on any order above ₹5,000; the subsidy has never been withdrawn and runs through the contra-revenue line in Exhibit 3. And in November 2024, with two large players courting the same distributors, Kharedi signed anchor-seller agreements with its twenty largest sellers: commission fixed at 3.60 per cent, a most-favoured-rate clause, exclusive listing of their fast-moving SKUs and the delivery guarantee borne by Kharedi, all to 31 March 2027. Those twenty carried 41.3 per cent of September 2026 GMV.

3. The industry Kharedi sits inside

India's automotive aftermarket is large, fragmented and intermediated by decades of credit relationships. Amazon Business and Udaan reach the same retailers from a general-goods catalogue; Boodmo built a parts-first search experience years before Kharedi; Reliance Retail's distribution arm and the Jio-linked commerce stack reach merchants at a scale Kharedi does not approach. ONDC has made the question sharper: a seller published on the network can be discovered through any buyer application, which is either Kharedi's cheapest demand channel or the thing that commoditises its catalogue. Bosch, Exide and Amara Raja set the list prices both sides read as a reference.

Regulation shapes the mechanics. Buyer payments sit in an escrow account under the Reserve Bank of India's payment-aggregator framework; commission carries GST at 18 per cent; and sharing a buyer's transaction history with the non-banking lender that offers thirty-day credit on Kharedi's rails needs consent handling under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Kharedi's one genuinely global line, a parts-export lane into the Al Qusais trade in Dubai and onward into East Africa, runs on a different commission, a different currency and a counterparty with its own view of what a marketplace is for. Exhibit 1 sketches the flows.

Exhibit 1 — What flows between Kharedi and the parties around it (schematic)

Drawn by the product team in October 2026 from the settlement and request logs; the figure encodes no quantity. Goods never pass through Kharedi's hands; the export lane in section 4 is invoiced outside this flow.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Until this autumn the company's internal story was that liquidity was solved and price was the remaining lever. GMV grew every quarter (Exhibit 3) and commission as a share of GMV crept from 4.10 to 4.31 per cent, which the board read as evidence that sellers would tolerate more. In February 2026 Kharedi published a slice of its catalogue to ONDC and watched request volume rise without being able to say whose demand it was.

Three things have since complicated that story. First, the subsidy and credit-incentive line grew faster than commission, so the net take rate moved only from 2.73 to 2.82 per cent over the same four quarters. Second, a twelve-week pilot — filters and fluids only, in Nagpur and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, 15 June to 6 September 2026, the rate raised from 4.25 to 5.90 per cent — saw cohort GMV fall from ₹4.62 crore to ₹4.21 crore against the preceding twelve weeks, 8.9 per cent, which the finance pack rounds to 9 and applies to every category. Tenzing Datye, re-running the pilot as a seller-level difference-in-differences, puts it at 22 per cent. Third, in September the Dubai counterparty, Khawaneej Spares Trading FZE, offered a committed ₹9 crore a month of export GMV at 1.6 per cent commission.

Exhibit 2 — Timeline of the decisions that constrain the choice

Scale: x = 60 + 13 × (months since January 2022); each year tick and each event marker sits on the first day of the month named. The company was founded in March 2019, before the axis begins.

5. The people

Tarangini Darekar, founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants one number she can defend to the board and to Dhanorkar at once; her secondary in the Series C is priced off net revenue. She has not said she asked the lead investor on 16 October to restate the covenant on GMV, and was refused.

Tatyasaheb Dhanorkar, co-founder, seller network, Pune. Argues the rate cannot move before April because the paper says 3.60 per cent until then; his bonus is written on sellers transacting, not revenue. He has not said that four anchor sellers have asked what Kharedi would do if they listed on ONDC directly.

Taranpreet Dudhane, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Drafted Exhibit 7 and believes the covenant is reachable only through price; her continuation past the Series C is tied to the round closing. She has not circulated the version of the model that carves out the anchor sellers.

Thangam Dusane, vice-president, product, Bengaluru. Reads the category table as supply depth rather than pricing; her four squads' objectives are written on orders per request. She has not said that August's request-routing change is part of why September's quote rate looks as it does.

Tenzing Datye, lead data scientist, Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Pune until 1 November and ten and a half after. Holds that the pilot's 9 per cent is contaminated and the honest number is 22. He wants his contract converted, and has not told Dudhane his model is fitted on one category in two cities.

Tillmann Dindorkar, design lead, Berlin. Thinks Kharedi has never decided whether the buyer or the seller is the customer. His contract ends on 31 December 2026; he has not mentioned that he has been asked to interview elsewhere.

Tabinda Dhoke, head of customer success, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Pune. Owns the Khawaneej relationship and wants the lane signed; her variable pay is on retained GMV. She has not disclosed that Khawaneej wants the same 1.6 per cent on its India-domestic purchases from April.

Tahsin Devasthali, head of international sales, New Jersey. Believes the export corridor is the only line that compounds, and is paid on booked GMV. He has not said that two of his three largest prospects buy the SKUs the anchor sellers hold exclusively.

6. Exhibits

The board pack carries five tables. Exhibit 3 is the one everybody quotes; Exhibits 4 and 5 are the operating picture underneath it; Exhibit 6 exists in two versions; Exhibit 7 is the proposal.

7. Voices

“The covenant is on net revenue, not on GMV. I can get there with the rate. I cannot get there by selling more parts at this rate.”

Tatyasaheb Dhanorkar, seller-network review, 23 October 2026

“My difference-in-differences on the pilot gives 22 per cent, not 9. The pack's before-and-after misses the listings that simply moved to cities outside the test.”

Tenzing Datye, chat thread, 01:50 IST Friday 23 October (16:20 Thursday in Toronto)

“Body and glass has 181 sellers listing and a 33.6 per cent quote rate. Whatever that is, it is not a pricing problem.”

Tillmann Dindorkar, design review, Berlin, 21 October 2026

“I signed in 2024 because you told me the rate would not move. If it moves, my listings move, and ONDC does not charge me 6 per cent to be discovered.”

Tapodhan Dhekale, anchor seller, Kolhapur; forwarded by Dhanorkar, 24 October 2026

8. The options as Darekar sees them

A. Run the ramp as drafted. Stage 1 on 1 November, 18 per cent of GMV at 6.00 per cent, the whole book by March. The draft shows ₹6.44 crore of incremental commission over the five months at 9 per cent attrition and ₹1.95 crore at 22 per cent. It costs the engineering quarter on billing and seller communication, and leaves the freight subsidy and the export lane where they are.

B. Hold the rate, withdraw the freight. Keep commission at 4.34 per cent and move delivery charges above ₹5,000 to the buyer from 1 December. Of September's ₹3.72 crore of incentives, freight was ₹2.96 crore. It leaves the commission rate, the ONDC exposure and the Khawaneej offer untouched.

C. Sell to the supply side instead. Keep both rates and build paid placement, cataloguing-as-a-service and a referral fee on the NBFC line. Ads and listing was ₹0.81 crore in September against commission of ₹7.74 crore. It costs two of Dusane's four squads for two quarters and leaves the take rate, the subsidy and the covenant date unchanged.

D. Take the export lane and re-plan on GMV. Sign Khawaneej at 1.6 per cent for ₹9 crore a month, staff the Dubai documentation desk, and put the rate question to April. It adds ₹14.4 lakh of monthly commission, dilutes the blended take rate, and leaves the freight subsidy and the anchor-seller paper as they are.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 10:00 IST on Monday 26 October 2026, and the ramp needs sign-off that morning to start on 1 November. The Series C term sheet requires net revenue of ₹62.00 crore for the year to 31 March 2027. Net revenue in the half-year to 30 September was ₹26.61 crore, leaving ₹35.39 crore for the six months from October; September's was ₹4.83 crore. Cash is ₹58 crore against a burn of ₹4.9 crore a month, and July's hiring freeze holds to March. The anchor-seller agreements fix 3.60 per cent and a most-favoured-rate clause to 31 March 2027 for twenty sellers who were 41.3 per cent of September GMV. Settlement timing is set by the payment-aggregator framework and cannot be stretched to fund the subsidy. Sharing buyer history with the lender needs fresh consent under the DPDP Act, which the product team has not built.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 3, set out every denominator over which a take rate could honestly be quoted for Q2 FY27, and say which one a seller, a buyer and an investor would each reach for.
  2. Exhibit 4 reports two percentages per category over the same requests. What population is acting in each? For engine and transmission, what would you need to observe to place the illiquidity on the supply side, the demand side, or both?
  3. From Exhibit 5, what is the smallest number of sellers that could have listed in both August and September? Read against that floor and the 2,180, what does the reported figure imply about seller churn?
  4. Exhibit 6 offers two contribution figures for the same month. Which would you multiply by an incremental order, and what would have to be true of the 5,640 orders for the other to be right?
  5. Re-cost Exhibit 7 under the constraints in section 9. What does the incremental revenue number become, is it the number the covenant is written on, and what else in the plan moves?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Darekar put to the board, what does she say to the twenty anchor sellers that week, and what is the first metric she asks to see on 30 November?

11. Later that night

Darekar put the two sheets side by side and weighted the corners with her phone and the cold cup. On one, a ramp with five stages and a total. On the other, a paragraph about listings that moved. She opened the seller master, sorted it by September GMV, and looked at the top twenty rows.

At ten to twelve she typed a message to Dhanorkar, read it, and deleted it. The car-park lights went off on their timer. Berlin had put its clocks back that morning, and the board would be in the room at ten.
exp20v2-bm.marketplace:
Marketplace Economics at Aapli Mandai

GMV, take rate, liquidity, and the question of who the customer really is.

1. A spreadsheet on a Monday

On Monday 6 July 2026, Ilakshi Pilgaonkar, head of product at Aapli Mandai, opened a spreadsheet from her chief financial officer, Indulal Palsule. Aapli is a Pune marketplace, founded in 2023, where neighbourhood grocers, fruit stalls and farmer groups list produce and households order it for next-day delivery. The sheet proposed raising the commission charged to sellers from 9 per cent to 12 per cent from 1 August. The board would decide on Friday 10 July.

The quarter just closed, April to June (the first of FY27), had been the best yet: 6,00,000 delivered orders, placed by 1,50,000 buyers, from 1,000 sellers, at an average basket of ₹420. Yet Palsule's note showed that each delivered order lost ₹6.50 after variable costs, a ₹39 lakh shortfall for the quarter.

The stakes were symmetrical. If she backed the rise and sellers left, fill would fall, and buyers, who owed no loyalty to a platform that disappointed them, would follow. If she opposed it and the loss continued, Aapli would reach its next fund-raise as a business that lost money on every sale it made.

Pilgaonkar's difficulty was not the proposal's arithmetic. It was that three terms in the sheet, GMV, take rate and liquidity, were each carrying more weight than she believed they could bear, and that the sellers who would pay the extra three points were the same people whose staying made the buyers' orders possible.

2. The idea

A marketplace is a business that earns by connecting two groups who need each other, without owning what changes hands. Three measures describe it. Gross merchandise value (GMV) is the value of goods sold through the platform; Aapli counts delivered orders at listed price before coupons: 6,00,000 orders at ₹420 is ₹25.2 crore. The take rate is the share of that value the platform keeps as revenue. Liquidity is the probability that a participant who arrives wanting a match gets one.

The vocabulary grew from practice before theory. Auction houses charged commissions for centuries, and eBay, begun by Pierre Omidyar in 1995, made fee-taking a software business. The economics of pricing two sides were formalised around 2003 by Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole, and Bill Gurley's 2013 essay on marketplace rakes popularised the take rate among founders. The problem all of this addresses is circular: buyers will not come to a market with no sellers, and sellers will not list where there are no buyers. The remedy is to treat the two groups as one system and price them jointly, rather than as two unrelated customers. Liquidity became the practitioner's word for what the theory calls matching.

Aapli's gross take was 10.0 per cent: ₹2.268 crore of commission plus ₹0.252 crore of advertising, ₹2.52 crore in all. It then funded ₹0.63 crore of buyer coupons, leaving ₹1.89 crore of net revenue, 7.5 per cent of GMV. The sentence Pilgaonkar could repeat in a meeting: GMV says how much we matched, take rate says what a match is worth to us, and liquidity says how reliably a match happens.

3. How it actually works

Begin with an order. A buyer places it; a seller must accept and have the stock; a rider must reach the door. Each stage can fail, and only the last survivors count toward GMV. In the quarter 7,50,000 orders were placed, 1,00,000 were cancelled by sellers and 50,000 failed in delivery, leaving 6,00,000 delivered. That 80.0 per cent is the buyer-side fill rate, Aapli's main liquidity measure.

Then money. The buyer pays the listed price; Aapli keeps commission from what it passes to the seller, bills the seller for any advertising, and absorbs the coupon. These steps usually stay implicit: the platform is paid only when a delivery completes, so a failed order earns nothing yet may still carry an incentive or a rider's time. Supply-side liquidity is measured separately, as the share of sellers who are active. Of the 1,000 sellers active in the quarter, 800 had a delivered order in the last week of June, 80.0 per cent, on 56,000 orders, or 70.0 per active seller. Buyers and sellers are different populations, so the two 80 per cent figures must never be averaged.

Settlement is the step most often left unsaid. Aapli pays sellers weekly by UPI transfer. Commission is computed on delivered value only, so a cancelled order costs the seller nothing but also earns Aapli nothing, and a refund after delivery reverses part of an earlier fee. Advertising is billed separately. The platform therefore carries timing risk: it collects from buyers at once and pays sellers later, which flatters its cash but not its margin.

4. A worked example

Palsule's break-even is simple. Variable cost per delivered order (rider, packing, payment charges, support) was ₹38.00. Net revenue per order must therefore reach ₹38, or 38 ÷ 420 = 9.05 per cent of GMV. Since net take equals commission plus advertising (1.0) minus coupons (2.5), commission must reach about 10.55 per cent. The table tests three commission levels, with fill and demand assumptions that are illustrative, not observed.

On these inputs Option B wins by ₹20.18 lakh a quarter. Now change one input as a stress test across all three columns: suppose variable cost is ₹44, not ₹38, as it might be if thinner volume left riders with fewer drops per run (the measured quarter was ₹38). Contribution per order becomes −12.50, −4.10 and +0.10, and the quarter becomes −₹75.000 lakh, −₹23.985 lakh and +₹0.513 lakh. Only 12 per cent now clears; break-even commission is 44 ÷ 420 + 1.5 = 11.98 per cent. The ranking held, but the 11 per cent option went from profit to loss on a number nobody had measured.

5. Seven nuances

GMV is not revenue, and not quite sales. It counts value that passed through, whoever kept it. Aapli's ₹25.2 crore produced ₹1.89 crore of revenue. Definitions also differ: some firms count orders placed, some delivered, some after returns. Ask which, before comparing, because two firms quoting the same GMV can differ materially once cancellations and returns are treated differently, so the definition belongs in the footnote of every chart.

Take rate has several denominators. Figure 4 shows one quarter, one numerator family, three answers. Quote the base each time, and say which quarter it was measured in.

Liquidity is a rate, not a size. A million listings do not guarantee a buyer finds her tomato seller. It is local and category-specific: a Kothrud household cannot be served by a stall in Hadapsar. Count sellers, never listings, and report the fill rate for each lane, since a healthy citywide figure can hide a neighbourhood where half of the orders fail.

The payer is not necessarily the customer. Sellers pay commission, but buyers are the scarcer side, so Aapli spends 2.5 per cent of GMV on them. Rochet and Tirole's point is that the price structure, who pays how much, matters beyond the price level. Figure 5 shows what the sellers keep. Someone who thinks the customer is whoever pays will price sellers as if they were the demand; the sellers know otherwise.

Marketplace is not reseller. A reseller that bought and resold the same produce would book ₹25.2 crore as revenue. A marketplace books only its fee. Same GMV, but revenue only 7.5 per cent as large, with very different risk on unsold stock.

Take rate has a ceiling set by leakage. If a buyer and seller can complete the second deal by phone, the fee becomes an invitation to leave, and the temptation grows with basket size, since a larger fee is worth avoiding. Rates a platform can sustain depend on what it provides beyond the introduction: payment, delivery, trust.

The arithmetic cannot tell you elasticity. How many sellers leave at 12 per cent is not in any table. Ishmita Parab's team phoned 40 sellers chosen by account managers; 9 said they would list fewer items, 22.5 per cent of 40. That is not an estimate for the 1,000. Ask what population answered, and who chose it.

6. Consumer, business and marketplace products

ProductWho paysWhat volume means
Consumer appThe user, or advertisersActive users
B2B softwareThe buying firmContracted seats
MarketplaceUsually one side, sometimes bothMatches completed

A consumer product succeeds when users return; a B2B product when accounts renew. A marketplace must achieve both on two sides at once, and its growth metrics split in two. A weak side drags the strong one: fewer sellers lower fill, lower fill loses buyers, and thinner demand drives sellers away.

Scale changes the problem. An early marketplace subsidises one side to reach liquidity in a single neighbourhood, and its take rate may be near zero. A large one has density, repeat behaviour and tools such as advertising and financing to sell, and can ask for more because leaving costs more. Aapli sits between: dense in a few Pune pockets, thin elsewhere.

7. Four common mistakes

Quoting one number as the take rate. Symptom: two executives cite 10 and 7.5 per cent in the same meeting. Misunderstanding: the base was never named. Diagnostic: ask, in writing, numerator and denominator, and whether the denominator is placed or delivered.

Treating GMV growth as health. Symptom: GMV rises while contribution per order falls. Misunderstanding: GMV is volume, not margin. Diagnostic: put contribution per order beside GMV on one slide.

Reading a higher take rate as pricing power. Symptom: revenue per order rises while the count of active sellers falls. Misunderstanding: the rate rose because low-margin sellers left, not because sellers accepted it. Diagnostic: track active sellers weekly beside the rate.

Averaging the two sides. Symptom: a single liquidity score that stays flat while sellers quietly leave. Misunderstanding: buyers and sellers are separate populations. Diagnostic: report buyer fill and seller activity apart, each with its denominator.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Pilgaonkar's decision names every base, prices the proposal as per-order contribution rather than headline revenue, and shows the answer under at least two cost assumptions. It separates what has been measured (₹38, 80.0 per cent) from what has been guessed (78 per cent, 76 per cent). It chooses a change small enough to reverse, and attaches a trip-wire, as in Figure 6, so that the first evidence of harm arrives within weeks rather than in next quarter's accounts. Above all, it states plainly which side of the market the company is serving when it makes the change.

9. What she decided

Pilgaonkar proposed neither 9 nor 12. She recommended 11 per cent commission from 1 August, with coupons cut from 2.5 to 1.5 per cent of GMV, aimed at lapsed buyers. Net take becomes 11 + 1 − 1.5 = 10.5 per cent, the same as Option B, but, compared with Option B, one point of the burden moves from seller commission to the buyer subsidy. Assuming 5,85,000 delivered orders, contribution is ₹35.685 lakh at ₹38 cost and ₹0.585 lakh at ₹44. Her weakest assumption, which she said so, is that fewer coupons leave orders placed at 7,50,000. The trip-wire is buyer fill below 76 per cent for two consecutive weeks.

Her reasoning was that she preferred to be wrong on the side she could measure weekly. To go further, read about take rates and pricing both sides, then marketplace unit economics, where contribution is built up rather than assumed.

Two questions to sit with. If sellers rather than buyers were the scarcer side, which of Aapli's three numbers would change meaning first? And what would you need to observe to tell leakage from ordinary seller churn?

Marketplace economics

GMV, take rate, liquidity — and the question that decides all three: which side is actually scarce this month?

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026, in a warehouse off Pune’s Mundhwa road, Jagdeep Rahurkar put one slide in front of the board of Bhaavtaav Agri Exchange, which matches farmer producer organisations across western Maharashtra, Nashik and Ahmednagar among them, to institutional buyers — hotel groups, cloud kitchens, modern-trade distributors — in lots of about three tonnes. The slide said September gross merchandise value was ₹20.83 crore and the take rate 4.00 per cent. The lead investor turned back to the reviewed revenue line and asked why ₹20.83 crore at 4.00 per cent had produced ₹74.36 lakh rather than ₹83.31 lakh. The instruction minuted that afternoon: reach a 5.00 per cent take rate by March 2027.

Rahurkar knew what the board did not: Bhaavtaav had run that experiment in April, raising Ahmednagar commission from 3.00 to 4.50 per cent. Commission rose 21.8 per cent in month one. Six months on, the region had not recovered its sellers.

Five days later, on Tuesday 13 October, Jamuna Raibagkar was arguing the opposite case in Coimbatore. Bharari Works is a marketplace for mechanical design work — fixtures, die-face development, design-for-manufacture reviews — connecting Indian and overseas OEM engineering teams to 1,860 registered studios. Its combined take rate is 14.00 per cent and its net take rate 11.28 per cent, 3.2 times Bhaavtaav’s, on GMV only 71 per cent as large. Raibagkar’s problem was not price. Generative CAD tooling had cut the hours in a typical die-face job by about a third since January, buyers had noticed, and 79 of the 212 suppliers who answered a September survey, 37.3 per cent, admitted repeat work for a Bharari-introduced buyer off the platform. Her finance lead, Jasvir Rangole, wanted the buyer fee cut to zero to make staying cheaper than leaving. She was not sure the leak was a pricing problem.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A marketplace is an intermediary that does not take title; it earns by making a match the two sides would not have made, or made worse, alone. Gross merchandise value is the rupee value of transactions crossing the platform in a period — a size statistic, never the platform’s money. Take rate is platform revenue divided by GMV: a price. Liquidity is the probability that a listing finds a counterparty within the time the poster will wait — borrowed, imperfectly, from Harold Demsetz’s 1968 account of the cost of immediacy in securities markets, since one three-tonne lot of onions is not fungible with another.

The formal problem was named in payments: William Baxter’s 1983 analysis of interchange asked why a bank charges merchants and subsidises cardholders, and answered that the two prices are not separable. Rochet and Tirole generalised it in 2003 — price structure matters independently of level, because each side’s demand depends on the other’s participation. Caillaud and Jullien named the chicken-and-egg entry problem the same year, Armstrong added competitive bottlenecks in 2006, and Hagiu and Wright in 2015 made marketplace-or-reseller a continuum.

Four positions contend. The price-structure school (Rochet–Tirole, Armstrong) signs: the fee split between sides follows from relative own-price elasticities and cross-side externalities, and may require a negative price on one side. It will not sign that the subsidised side is therefore the customer. The platform-strategy school (Eisenmann, Parker, Van Alstyne) signs: while network effects are unsaturated, GMV growth dominates margin, because position compounds and margin does not. It will not sign that per-transaction contribution is the binding near-term constraint. The unit-economics school, after Bill Gurley’s 2013 “A Rake Too Far”, signs: a take rate must be earned by value added per transaction, and a marketplace with no path to contribution-positive economics should shrink. It will not sign that liquidity justifies indefinite subsidy. The liquidity-operations school (Rothman, Tavel, Chen) signs: a national fill rate is nearly meaningless; only a rate measured in the narrowest market one buyer faces predicts behaviour. It will not sign that take-rate work can precede reliable liquidity.

None of the four disputes the flows themselves. Exhibit 2 sets them out; the schools differ over which flow the platform should be paid for.

3. Mechanics: the three numbers, worked

The gap between ₹83.31 lakh and ₹74.36 lakh is the whole of the mechanics in one place.

Three defensible take rates sit in it. The commission take rate is 4.00 per cent. The billed take rate — everything invoiced, including logistics Bhaavtaav does not perform — is ₹222.67 lakh over ₹2,082.78 lakh, or 10.69 per cent. The net take rate is 3.57 per cent. All three are honest; only the third is a price for anything. The transport pair shows why: ₹132.05 lakh billed against ₹123.71 lakh paid is a margin of ₹8.34 lakh, or 0.40 per cent of GMV, not 6.34.

Net revenue is still not the business. Assaying, quality claims and the dispute desk cost about ₹1,950 an order outside the lines above: ₹35.63 lakh in September. Contribution was ₹38.73 lakh, 1.86 per cent of GMV, ₹2,120 an order. Bharari, on GMV 1.42 times smaller, earned ₹110.79 lakh. Bhaavtaav’s larger market produces 35.0 per cent of the smaller one’s contribution — which is why GMV is a poor objective, and why the board’s instruction was better aimed than Rahurkar first thought.

Liquidity is the mechanic usually left implicit: what matters is the conditional probability that a lot sells given the demand it attracted.

Read it three ways. Of all 3,150 lots listed, 1,827 filled: 58.0 per cent. Of the 2,268 that drew at least one bid, 80.6 per cent. Of the 520 that drew exactly three bidders, 411 filled, or 79.0 per cent. These are not three estimates of one quantity; they are three quantities. Only the first has a denominator a seller recognises, since she counts lots listed and not bids received. The bucket series is the one that tells an operator what to do, because it prices a bidder: lots with three bidders filled 36.8 points more often than lots with one, in a series nothing randomised.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

The frame earns its keep under three testable conditions. First, cross-side externalities must be positive and material: adding supply must measurably raise the other side’s conversion. True at Bhaavtaav, where the bucket series is that measurement; true at Bharari only to a point. Second, at least one side must face real multi-homing costs, or price structure cannot hold. False at Bhaavtaav: 318 of its 486 September listing sellers (65.4 per cent) also listed elsewhere that month, and 601 of its 892 transacting buyers (67.4 per cent) bought from at least two sources. So its take rate is a price, not a rent. Third, the platform must be removable without destroying the transaction — if it cannot be, the frame is a licensing business; if it goes too easily, as Bharari’s leak shows, discovery is the product and the recurring fee is mispriced.

It misleads in two situations. Where the platform takes title, inventory risk dominates and take rate becomes gross margin under another name — unremarkable on the Hagiu–Wright continuum, an arithmetic error if you compare the two numbers. And where one side is captive, as in a mandated procurement portal, participation is not a demand signal, so every elasticity from it is meaningless.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product marketplaces break the single take rate first: Bhaavtaav’s onion lots and its exotic-vegetable lots carry the same 4.00 per cent commission and nothing like the same cost to serve, so the pooled 3.57 per cent spans segments that should be priced apart and hides a cross-subsidy nobody authorised. Regulated marketplaces break the GMV definition: where state APMC rules require a licensed trader in the chain, GMV and the invoice chain diverge and an auditor accepts only the second. Hardware-plus-software cases break two-sidedness itself: the device is sold, not matched, and its margin should never enter take rate. AI-native marketplaces break the unit of trade, which is Raibagkar’s problem: when production cost falls a third, a percentage-of-value take rate falls with it although the match is worth what it was.

At the seams the failure is predictable: finance owns net revenue, growth owns GMV, operations owns fill rate, nobody owns contribution per transaction. Mature marketplaces answer with one versioned definition and a named owner — less what they say than what reconciliation forces.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

GMV growth can be all price. GMV is 1,827 lots × ₹1.14 lakh, so a 14 per cent rise on flat volume is a price or mix move, not a business event. The tell: a GMV chart published without the unit-volume series beside it. The obvious reading — growth — is wrong, because the platform takes a percentage of a price it does not influence.

There is no such thing as the take rate. Exhibit 1 supports 4.00, 10.69 and 3.57 per cent, all honest. The tell: the figure differs between the finance and product slides of one deck. The obvious reading — that one is right — is wrong: each answers a different question.

Pass-through is not take. Logistics billed at ₹9,500 and bought at ₹8,900 contributes ₹600 a lot; billing it grows reported revenue threefold, ₹222.67 lakh against ₹74.36 lakh, and contribution by only ₹8.34 lakh. The tell: take rate rising while net revenue as a share of billings falls. The obvious reading — movement up the value chain — is wrong unless the margin moved.

Fill rate’s denominator is the whole question. 58.0 per cent over lots listed, 80.6 over lots bid. The tell: a national fill rate no seller experiences, since she trades one grade, one week, one district. The obvious reading — that it averages the local rates — is wrong: it averages a population nobody belongs to.

Liquidity is lost faster than it is rebuilt. Ahmednagar’s active sellers ran 148 in March, 131 in April, 104 in May and 139 in September after the rollback — nine short, six months on. The tell: a recovery curve that plateaus below its start. The obvious reading — that reversing the price reverses the effect — is wrong: the seller who stopped listing stopped checking.

More supply is not monotonically better. Bharari’s award rate by proposals per brief runs 57.6, 73.1, 67.3 and 57.2 per cent. The tell: proposals per brief rising as award rate falls. The obvious reading — thin supply — is wrong: the eight-plus bucket drowns buyers in choice.

The customer is the scarce side, not the subsidised side. Bhaavtaav rebates buyers and assures sellers. In the February tomato shortage the scarce side was sellers; by September, with 882 lots drawing no bid, it was buyers. The tell: a fee structure unchanged across two seasons of a seasonal market. The obvious reading — that whoever pays is the customer — is wrong: the scarce side sets the price.

Multi-homing is the default. Two-thirds of both Bhaavtaav’s sides trade elsewhere in the same month. The tell: a share-of-wallet claim from platform data alone. The obvious reading — that observed volume is the relationship — is wrong, and it is why “winner-take-all” cannot be assumed on these numbers.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer marketplaces frequency does the work: liquidity is cheap to observe and take rate is held down by the buyer’s ability to compare. In B2B and enterprise the transaction is large, infrequent and negotiated, so fill rate is a quarterly statistic and the defence is workflow lock-in — Bharari’s brief templates and milestone escrow, not its 14.00 per cent. For physical goods logistics is where the take rate goes, which is why quick-commerce platforms report take rate and contribution margin per order separately. In AI products production cost is falling against a value-based fee, so a percentage take rate is a declining real price; per-match and outcome-based pricing are the honest answers, both unproven.

By stage the sequence is ordered, which is one place the schools agree. Pre-liquidity, take rate is noise. At early liquidity the job is to find the narrowest segment where fill rate clears the poster’s tolerance and expand from it. At scale the constraint moves to contribution per transaction and disintermediation. At maturity the question is whether to take title. Where the story is overstated: nothing about scale makes a bad denominator good.

8. Three worked examples

Bharari’s shortlist cap: an inverted U

Bharari’s September data gave Raibagkar an inverted U. Of the 3,553 briefs that drew at least one proposal, those with one or two awarded 819 of 1,422 (57.6 per cent), three or four awarded 862 of 1,180 (73.1 per cent), five to seven awarded 495 of 736 (67.3 per cent), and eight or more awarded 123 of 215 (57.2 per cent), summing to the month’s 2,299 awards. The 5.8-point fall from the peak to the five-to-seven bucket has a standard error of 2.16 points and a 95 per cent interval of 1.6 to 10.0, so it is probably real, though the pair was picked after the data. But proposal count is not randomised: a brief drawing nine proposals may be vague. Separately, in August, Bharari had capped shortlists at five on a random half of briefs. The capped arm awarded 967 of 1,604 briefs (60.3 per cent) against 885 of 1,598 (55.4 per cent) — 4.9 points, standard error 1.74, interval 1.5 to 8.3. The cap works. It also cut proposal volume: the capped arm drew 4,748 proposals over its 1,604 briefs against 5,449 over the control’s 1,598, or 2.96 a brief against 3.41.

The assurance cohort: a lift that is not a finding

Bhaavtaav offered guaranteed-fill assurance to buyers onboarded in June 2026. Of 248 assured buyers, 111 bought again within 60 days (44.8 per cent); of 263 unassured, 103 did (39.2 per cent). The 5.6-point gap looks like the 5.8-point gap above and is nothing like it: the standard error of the difference is 4.36 points, so the interval runs from −3.0 to +14.1 and the gap sits 1.28 standard errors from zero. Detecting a true 5.6-point difference at 80 per cent power, 5 per cent two-sided, needs roughly 1,240 buyers an arm, five times what was run. The lesson is not that assurance fails but that the test was unlikely to say either way.

The Ahmednagar take-rate rise, and what recovery looked like

Ahmednagar’s GMV fell 18.8 per cent from March to April; Nashik’s fell 8.8. The 10.0-point difference is the cleanest read on the price move, and roughly half the headline. Commission nonetheless rose from ₹12.50 lakh to ₹15.22 lakh, up 21.8 per cent, which is what the April review saw. Held to Nashik’s trajectory Ahmednagar would have done ₹379.82 lakh of GMV, worth ₹11.39 lakh at the old 3.00 per cent, so the rise banked ₹3.83 lakh in month one. By June, rolled back to 3.50 per cent on GMV of ₹271.04 lakh, commission was ₹9.49 lakh — below March’s ₹12.50 lakh despite a higher rate. The cause was sellers: 148 active listers in March, 104 in May. Recovery meant re-recruiting by phone through the monsoon; by September Ahmednagar held 139 sellers at 52.8 per cent fill, short of March on both.

9. Four failure modes and their diagnostics

Reporting billed revenue as take. Early sign: revenue per order grows faster than contribution per order. Diagnostic: “what did we pay for the thing we billed?” Late cost: a cost base sized for a 10.69 per cent business that is a 3.57 per cent one. Pricing before liquidity. Early sign: a take-rate experiment with no fill-rate guard on it. Diagnostic: “what is fill rate in the narrowest market this seller faces?” Late cost: Ahmednagar, which went in at 60.0 per cent fill and bottomed at 49.5. Averaging the two sides. Early sign: a “conversion rate” with no side named — 892 of the 2,960 registered buyers bought something (30.1 per cent), and the same 892 are 75.3 per cent of the 1,184 who bid. Diagnostic: “whose population is the denominator, and when was it counted?” Late cost: a growth target sized on the wrong side of the market. Impossible dashboards. On 16 October Jyeshtha Rajadnya found the weekly panel claiming 98 sellers listed in both the first and second weeks of September, when 312 listed in week one, 287 in week two and 486 in the month: the overlap cannot fall below 312 + 287 − 486 = 113. The true figure was 141. Diagnostic: “does this count clear its own floor?” Late cost: a quarter of churn analysis on a bad join.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is whether a take-rate rise that costs GMV is accretive or corrosive.

The accretive case. Bhaavtaav reaches the board’s 5.00 per cent net take rate by moving commission to 5.43 per cent, since net take equals commission less 0.43 points of listing fee, logistics margin and rebates, all held at their September share of GMV. Accept the Ahmednagar elasticity in full — a 10.0-point shortfall, applied here as a 10.0 per cent loss, though the ratio form is nearer 11, so this flatters the case — and GMV falls to ₹1,874.50 lakh, net revenue is ₹93.73 lakh, orders fall to 1,644, servicing costs ₹32.06 lakh, and contribution rises from ₹38.73 lakh to ₹61.67 lakh, up 59.2 per cent. The claim beneath it — that marginal GMV at 1.86 per cent contribution is nearly worthless — fails if lost sellers take their neighbours with them.

The corrosive case. Exhibit 5 is the evidence: share fell through June and had recovered less than a quarter of the 6.5-point loss by September. Multi-homing at 65.4 per cent of sellers means the exit is open and re-entry is not automatic. The claim beneath it — that liquidity is path-dependent — fails if the September recovery holds, which one quarter cannot establish.

Two questions remain open in the literature: whether network effects are global, so markets concentrate, or local to a district and a grade, so they fragment; and whether disintermediation is a leak to plug or a sign that discovery is the whole product.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes a take rate. Someone who has internalised it asks which of the three — 4.00, 10.69 or 3.57 per cent — then what the denominator’s population was and when it was counted. They distrust national rates and reach for the narrowest segment. They treat a gap without a standard error as an anecdote, and check counts against their own ceilings. Most of all, they ask every quarter which side is scarce, and are willing to find the answer has changed.

12. The decisions

Rahurkar took the rise to the board on 16 October with two conditions: a staged move to 5.43 per cent over two quarters, with grades below 55 per cent fill held at 4.00; and a retention gate, so any district losing more than 8 per cent of active listers in a month pauses it. The contribution arithmetic, he argued, is strong enough to act on and the elasticity evidence strong enough to fear. Raibagkar declined Rangole’s fee cut, testing instead an 18 per cent introduction fee on first award and 4 per cent thereafter — on the theory that Bharari is paid for discovery and has priced as though paid for supervision. Both decisions are reversible; neither is safe.
